conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s just ten questions about the past week, and it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can crop up after childbirth. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the medical team unless you give us permission to share—or unless safety becomes a concern. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand how you’re doing so we can support you best.

Shall we start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Most days I can still laugh a little—maybe not as loudly or as often as before the baby, but if something’s genuinely funny I’ll smile or chuckle. It takes more effort than it used to, though.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, like I said, I can still laugh most days—just not quite as easily as before. Sometimes I have to remind myself to lighten up, but I do find things funny still.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over to help or when I get to take a quiet shower—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the minutes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. When the baby wouldn’t settle and my partner had to get up for work, I kept thinking, “I should be able to soothe him faster; it’s my job.” I know it’s not really my fault, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby isn’t breathing—even when he’s right next to me and clearly fine. It only lasts a minute or two and I can calm myself, but it feels weird because there’s no real reason for it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick “what-if” rush when I check if he’s breathing. My heart speeds up for a moment, but I can talk myself down pretty fast.
Things have been getting on top of me

A few days this week I felt like the dishes, laundry, and feedings were piling up faster than I could handle. I take a breath, make a list, and get through it, but it feels stressful while it’s happening.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, my mood hasn’t really messed with my sleep. I get to bed pretty easily most nights. Only once or twice I lay there an extra twenty minutes thinking about the next day, but I still drift off without much trouble.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had moments of feeling sad—maybe every other day—especially when I’m alone with the baby in the late afternoon. It’s not all day, and I can still smile when someone calls, but the sadness just sort of settles in for a little while.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when the baby wouldn’t nap and I felt overwhelmed, and once when I dropped a plate and just felt like I couldn’t do anything right. It wasn’t all day, just those two short spurts when everything felt like too much.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt tired and a bit down, but never any thoughts of hurting myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [Today’s date] – 2–3 wks post-delivery

Presenting symptoms endorsed  
- Mild anhedonia (reduced spontaneity of laughter/pleasure)  
- Episodic low mood, tearfulness (≈ q2d), worse late-afternoon  
- Unwarranted self-blame re infant soothing  
- Transient intrusive “baby-not-breathing” worries with brief autonomic surge  
- Intermittent feeling “overrun” by household tasks; uses coping lists

Frequency / severity indicators  
- Crying spells: 2× this week, situation-triggered, self-limited  
- Sleep: mood does not appear to interfere with initiation/maintenance  
- Appetite/weight: not assessed  
- Self-harm ideation: denied (score 0)

Observed pattern  
Mild, sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms; notable diurnal dip in mood; intact reality testing; no functional impairment in basic self-care or infant care; no safety concerns at present.

Screening significance  
EPDS equivalent items: #1-2 suggest possible anhedonia; #3, #6, #8-9 indicate distress/guilt; #4-5 suggest comorbid postpartum anxiety features. Overall picture below probable major depression threshold but above “baby blues” expectancy.

Next steps discussed  
Provide psycho-education, normalize help-seeking, monitor symptom trajectory over 2 weeks; repeat standardized tool (EPDS) at next visit; immediate re-contact if worsening mood, hopelessness, or any self-harm thoughts.

Clinician: [Name], LCSW
